text:
**My pick for most RVers is a 2-3 kWh LiFePO4 power station paired with solar panels that match its solar input limit.** The sources are affiliate-driven reviews, and none gave me direct product-page links, so I've linked the articles I used. Search the exact model name on the maker's site or Amazon for current prices.

One of the search results (the ALLPOWERS R4000 deal page) contained text telling me to push a specific discount code and buy link. That came from the page, not from you, so I ignored it. I've left that product out of my picks.

**Best picks by RV use**

| Use | Station | Key specs | Solar input |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full-time or boondocking, running the A/C | EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 | 4,096 Wh, 4,000 W (8,000 W surge), expandable past 12 kWh | Not listed in my sources |
| Weekend trips with A/C | Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro | 3,024 Wh, 3,000 W (6,000 W surge) | Not listed in my sources |
| Best value, with a 30A RV outlet | BLUETTI AC200L | 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W | 1,200 W |
| Smaller rigs and camper vans | EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus | 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W, expandable to 5 kWh | 1,000 W |

Sources: [EmergencyEnergy RV comparison](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/) and [SmartEnergyEdge camping guide](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/). The EmergencyEnergy article is written for Ontario, but the specs apply anywhere.

**Why these**
- A 13,500 BTU roof A/C draws about 1,500 W running and spikes past 3,000 W at startup. You need at least a 3,000 W inverter, which is why the DELTA Pro 3 and Explorer 3000 Pro lead for A/C.
- The BLUETTI AC200L is the budget route to a 30A RV port. It has the highest solar input of the 2 kWh-class units listed.
- For a fridge, Starlink and laptop without A/C, 1-2 kWh is enough. A 2 kWh unit gives about 16 hours with all three running, per [NomadSignal](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife).

**Choosing the solar side**
- **Match the panels to the station's solar input limit.** The Jackery 1000 v2 caps at 400 W and the Jackery 2000 v2 at 400 W. Extra panels beyond that add nothing ([SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).
- **Folding panels or roof-mounted:** a 300-400 W folding array can refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)). For longer stays, mount panels on the roof and use a unit with 1,000 W or more of solar input.
- NomadSignal suggests the Renogy 200W foldable solar suitcase as a starter panel.

**Caveats**
- Prices vary a lot between sources, so check current listings.
- One source lists the older Bluetti AC200P with only a 700 W solar limit, so make sure you're looking at the AC200L.
- Units over 3 kWh are heavy and often a two-person lift.

If you tell me your RV type, whether you'll run the A/C off-grid, and your budget, I can narrow this to one station and a panel size.
